rationale: One adult with late-diagnosed phenylketonuria had action and rest tremor and later parkinsonism. Childhood phenylalanine restriction partly improved speech. Adherence was limited after later reintroduction, and an attempt at stricter restriction was discontinued. Suspected visual hallucinations improved after pramipexole withdrawal. The later levodopa motor examination scored 32 off and 28 on. The clinician's observation, dietary history and drug sequence describe separate events. No visual episode count or dried fig comparison was made.

The review traces nucleus basalis of Meynert anatomy, postmortem cholinergic-cell loss and clinical associations in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. It discusses neuronal loss, occipitoparietal activity and other possible contributors to visual hallucinations. It offers neither a dietary comparison nor visual episode counts after dried fig exposure.

The chapter synthesizes auditory recognition, music processing, dementia and relevant neuroanatomy. Case examples concern how auditory symptoms and music-related abilities vary across dementias. Its sensory context does not measure dried fig exposure or visual hallucination frequency.

The review surveys genetic, biochemical and biological-fluid markers for aging-related neurocognitive disorders. Recurrent visual hallucinations are cited as a Lewy body dementia feature. The differential timing of cognitive and motor onset is diagnostic context. No dried fig contrast or measured effect on visual episodes is supplied.

The 27 Parkinson participants, 23 older controls and 20 younger adults judged two interpretations of an ambiguous Necker cube while visual cues and instructions varied. Outcome measures were percept dominance and alternation under passive or intentional viewing. The experiments test how participants respond to an external ambiguous image. Background discussion of hallucinations does not turn the task into a count of spontaneous visual episodes. No food was assigned.

Two families with OPA1 variants had syndromic neurological findings that included parkinsonism, dementia, optic or other sensory disturbances, and mitochondrial abnormalities. An individual case had clinical visual hallucinations. Clinical descriptions and functional assays do not establish a food-timed visual episode rate or transfer directly to idiopathic Parkinson disease.

CHCHD10 variant analysis covers several neurodegenerative diagnostic groups. One familial frontotemporal lobar degeneration case had visual hallucinations during clinical deterioration and developed bradykinesia later. The report is a genetic and differential-diagnosis inquiry. It supplies no fig exposure or longitudinal visual episode counts for Parkinson disease.

The review relates cognitive profiles and visual perceptual dysfunction in Parkinson dementia to large-scale neural networks. Its visual hallucination map refers to prior imaging contrasts and its discussion draws on earlier clinical and experimental studies. It does not add a new food-exposed cohort or count visual episodes after dried fig intake.

Cell and hemiparkinsonian rat experiments test the phosphodiesterase-7 inhibitor S14 and measure dopaminergic differentiation and neurogenesis-related outcomes. The introductory reference to visual hallucinations describes human Parkinson symptoms. The animal experiment has neither a fig comparison nor a hallucination assessment.

Resting functional MRI contrasts brain networks in dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer disease and controls. Clinical characterization recorded hallucination-related features in the Lewy body group. Connectivity differences are diagnostic and mechanistic measures. No assessed dietary factor or Parkinson visual episode rate is reported.

The review compares neurophysiological biomarkers, including EEG features and other modalities, for Lewy body dementias. Hallucinations are included in clinical and mechanistic context. The cited neurophysiology does not constitute a test of eating dried figs or an episode frequency comparison.

The study compares behavioral and psychological symptom scores in dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer disease by Clinical Dementia Rating stage. The Neuropsychiatric Inventory obtained caregiver information for the preceding month. The Lewy body group scored higher on the hallucination domain overall, with stage-specific analyses. The reported domain combines symptom characteristics and does not isolate longitudinal visual episode counts in Parkinson disease.

The investigators combine dopamine transporter SPECT and cardiac MIBG imaging in a differential diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer disease. The baseline clinical-characteristics table reports hallucination presence by diagnostic group alongside other clinical features. Diagnostic discrimination and clinical presence do not measure food exposure or episode frequency in Parkinson disease.

People with lateralized Parkinson disease and older controls walked with visual and motor conditions manipulated to distinguish explanations for veering. Veering is the measured outcome. An earlier association between gait freezing and visual symptoms appears in the introduction. Participants were not tested for a food-timed hallucination effect.

The article considers retinal, visual processing and ocular changes in schizophrenia and related settings. It uses visual hallucinations, optical measures and drug-associated perceptual phenomena in a differential context. It supplies no dried fig exposure or corresponding Parkinson episode measure.

The article synthesizes structural, functional and molecular imaging in Parkinson disease. It considers imaging correlates of motor and nonmotor features. Imaging contrasts and discussion of hallucinations do not measure outcomes after dietary fig consumption.

Two otherwise distinct extended-release carbidopa-levodopa trial programs included a six-week open-label conversion before their randomized phases. The 450 immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa starters had two discontinuations attributed to visual hallucinations (0.4%). The 110 levodopa/entacapone starters had one adverse-event discontinuation whose reported terms did not include hallucinations. These are conversion-stage discontinuation counts, not the total event incidence or a randomized comparison. The registries and randomized reports are separate within the two parent families. No food exposure was assigned.

The study compares people with mild cognitive impairment who later met criteria for dementia with Lewy bodies or Alzheimer disease. Visual hallucinations were recorded at the mild cognitive impairment stage in nine of 25 Lewy body converters and in one Alzheimer converter. The authors also measured cognitive and visuospatial task performance. The clinical count is the number of patients with the symptom, not the number of episodes. No dried fig exposure was compared.

Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer disease and control groups completed an attention and executive task during functional imaging. Behavioral and task-network outcomes were analyzed, while hallucination-related networks were discussed in the interpretation. There was no measured dietary exposure or visual episode rate.

The study compared EEG measures and network activity in an alpha-synuclein transgenic mouse model and in humans with dementia with Lewy bodies. Human visual hallucinations are part of the clinical rationale. Neither the neurophysiological measures nor the animal experiment count food-timed clinical visual episodes.

Systematic chart review of 2,446 people in a Danish hospital register distinguished idiopathic Parkinson disease from other forms of parkinsonism. The protocol considered hallucinations unrelated to medication and timing of cognition relative to motor symptoms when adjudicating diagnoses. Those criteria do not provide a dried fig exposure or clinical visual episode measure.

The investigators relate verbal memory and task-related activation or diffusion imaging in Parkinson disease. This is a cognitive and structural comparison. The paper does not test food consumption or a visual hallucination frequency endpoint.

Nine antipsychotic trials in Parkinson psychosis cover quetiapine, clozapine, olanzapine and pimavanserin. Effects and tolerability varied. Clozapine improved the summarized psychosis outcome versus placebo, while pooled quetiapine and olanzapine analyses did not show clear benefit. Broad psychosis scales and trial-level outcomes do not estimate a specific dried-food effect. The constituent trials provide distinct endpoints and should not be counted again as corroborating samples.

The article reviews clinical motor and neuropsychiatric features reported with GBA variants, including cognitive, psychiatric and hallucination-related phenotypes in some cohorts. It is a synthesis of group definitions and clinical risks. It reports no independently tested food exposure or visual episode rate after dried figs.

Purified harmine, single-vine Banisteriopsis caapi extract and customary mixed-plant ceremonial beverages are distinct preparations. Historical harmine reports had inconsistent tremor results. The viewpoint cites a 30-person 2001 controlled trial in which the extract improved a composite motor score while tremor worsened, and describes one transient visual hallucination. The primary 2001 paper labels that event as hallucinations of unspecified modality. A favorable historical use account, the trial and its later retelling are not independent demonstrations of the same effect. There is no dried fig intervention.

The report identifies an ATP13A2 nonsense variant in a person with juvenile-onset Kufor-Rakeb syndrome. Visual hallucinations are part of the classic phenotype in earlier reports, while this case had no reported hallucinations. That observation is a case phenotype in genetic parkinsonism and does not test a dried fig exposure.
